newsitem.title: UK: UK union blames Laura Ashley for closures.
newsitem.headline: UK union blames Laura Ashley for closures.

text.p: A major British trade union blamed planned job losses at factories run by fashion and textiles group Laura Ashley Holdings Plc on the failings of the management, not its workers.

Peter Booth, national secretary of the textiles group of the Transport and General Workers (T&G) union told Reuters: "They (the management) have organised and reorganised and reorganised again and all of these reorganisations have a fairly heavy cost to them."
The T&G represents workers at the two loss-making garment sewing factories at Caernarfon and Machynlleth in Wales which Laura Ashley proposes to close down.

Terming the cuts "scandalous", Booth said he suspected the job losses could be attributed more to the "high-flown business strategies" of the management team than the viability and efficiency of the plants, worked by skilled employees, many of whom were women.
The union said it was already discussing with the company ways of saving the threatened jobs.

"The company's reorganisations are justified by accountants and by very highly-paid executives -- another added cost, who come up with what seem like grand plans which work well on paper but which have less to do with the realities of the marketplace," Booth said.
Laura Ashley had had its "fingers burned" in the U.S. where it had had to cut back its expansion programme. "Now the workers were paying the price", he said.
The group had said in its trading statement the closure was part of a restructure plan that would affect about 190 employees, or five percent of its total workforce worldwide.
The company said it intended to source the clothes made at these two facilities overseas, in order to save costs and make quality improvements in quality.
The union is concerned the Laura Ashley layoffs are part of a bigger picture of future job losses in the British textile industry, which is renowned for its low salaries and poor working conditions.

Booth estimated 50,000 out of 370,000 textile manufacturing jobs could go in the next three years as retailers increased pressure for lower prices leading manufacturers to set up plants in areas such as North Africa or India where labour is cheap.
"It's a much wider issue. Textiles is the third largest industry in Britain in terms of employment," the T&G spokesman said.
